# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Oggianu_2020_atomoxetine"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Oggianu_2020_atomoxetine"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12480>
  (open access, PMC7020267)

# What this model is, and what it is not

Oggianu 2020 used the Simcyp simulator (version 14) to predict paediatric doses
of trazodone for insomnia and to ask whether atomoxetine, often co-prescribed
in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, would raise trazodone exposure by
inhibiting CYP3A4. The paper contains two compound models:

* **Trazodone** -- a Simcyp *full-PBPK* model (Table 1). Its distribution is
  carried by Simcyp's organ volumes, blood flows and predicted tissue
  partition coefficients, none of which are printed; the only distribution
  number the paper gives is the predicted steady-state volume of 1.0 L/kg.
  Supplementary Information S4 states that the model code "cannot be
  published". A compartmental reduction of this model fails against the
  paper's own predictions (see [below](#trazodone)), so it is not packaged.
* **Atomoxetine** -- a Simcyp *minimal-PBPK* model (Table 2) built as the
  interaction perpetrator. Its compound layer is complete: apparent oral
  clearance by CYP2D6 phenotype with a between-subject CV, absorption rate,
  fraction absorbed, blood-to-plasma ratio and a steady-state volume, with no
  single adjusting compartment. A minimal PBPK model without that compartment
  is a systemic compartment plus the liver, which gives mono-exponential
  disposition, so it reduces to a one-compartment oral model with no fitted
  parameter. That reduction is the model packaged here.

The reduction is built from the paper's inputs and checked against the
**paper's own predicted** steady-state Cmax and AUC (Supplementary Tables
S3.1, S3.2 and S3.4), not against the clinical observations.

# Population

The atomoxetine simulations used the Simcyp Caucasian healthy-volunteer
population, split into CYP2D6 extensive (EM) and poor (PM) metabolizers
(Supplementary Information S3):

* 20 mg twice daily for 7 days: 10 trials of 7 subjects, age 20-50 years, all
  male, EM and PM (observed data: Sauer 2003).
* 40 mg twice daily for 7 days: 10 trials of 8 subjects, age 20-50 years, 50%
  female, EM and PM (observed data: FDA Strattera clinical pharmacology
  review, study HFBJ).
* 60 mg twice daily for 12 days, PM only: 10 trials of 8 subjects, age 20-35
  years, 50% female (the midazolam interaction verification).
* Trazodone interaction: 10 trials of 10 subjects, age 20-50 years, 50% female,
  60 mg atomoxetine twice daily for 12 days with 150 mg trazodone on day 10.

The paper does not print the body-weight distribution of these trials; the
median adult body weight of its healthy-volunteer virtual population is 73 kg
(Table 4), which is used below.

# Source trace

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ka | 0.926 1/h | Table 2 (from the population-PK analysis of the FDA Strattera review) |
| Fraction absorbed | 1 | Table 2 |
| CL/F, CYP2D6 EM | 26.4 L/h, CV 55.7% | Table 2 |
| CL/F, CYP2D6 PM | 2.55 L/h, CV 18% | Table 2 |
| Vss | 0.71 L/kg (optimized; observed 0.85) | Table 2; Methods 'Atomoxetine model development' |
| Distribution model | Minimal PBPK, no single adjusting compartment | Table 2 'Model' |
| B:P | 0.605 | Table 2 |
| fu (plasma) | 0.02 | Table 2 (cancels in the reduction, see below) |
| CYP3A4 Ki | 34 uM, fu,mic 0.23 | Table 2; Supplementary S3.2.1 (documented, not encoded) |
| Hepatic blood flow QH | 90 L/h | Methods, text below Equation 2 |
| Liver weight | 1,648 g | Methods 'Estimation of CYP3A4-mediated metabolism for trazodone' |
| Reference body weight | 73 kg | Table 4, adult row |
| Well-stirred liver | Equations 1-2 | Methods |
| Predicted Cmax / AUC, 20 and 40 mg BID | Means | Table 3; Supplementary Tables S3.1, S3.2 |
| Predicted Cmax / AUC, 60 mg BID PM | Means | Supplementary Table S3.4 |

## The reduction

With fraction absorbed and gut availability both 1 and no renal clearance, the
well-stirred liver gives, in blood, `CL/F = fu,B x CLint`. Dividing the plasma
CL/F by B:P therefore gives `fu,B x CLint` directly, and the plasma fraction
unbound cancels:

```{r reduction}
bp <- 0.605
qh <- 90
reduce <- function(clpo) {
  clint_b <- clpo / bp
  fh <- qh / (qh + clint_b)
  c(CLpo = clpo, fH = fh, CL = fh * clpo)
}
knitr::kable(
  rbind(EM = reduce(26.4), PM = reduce(2.55)),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Systemic plasma clearance (L/h) and hepatic availability implied by the Table 2 CL/F."
)
vc_ref <- 0.71 * 73 - 1.648
vc_ref
```

The systemic volume is `Vss x body weight` less the liver, which the minimal
PBPK model holds as a separate compartment: `r round(vc_ref, 2)` L at 73 kg.

Simcyp treats a clearance entered with a CV as the arithmetic mean of a
log-normal distribution. The model therefore centres the individual CL/F on
`mean x exp(-sd^2 / 2)`, with `sd = sqrt(log(1 + CV^2))`, and a standard-normal
`etalcl` scaled by the phenotype-specific `sd`. With a CV of 55.7% in
extensive metabolizers this matters: the mean AUC of the population is about
31% above `dose / mean CL/F`, and the paper's predicted mean AUCs carry that
inflation.

# Virtual cohort

```{r cohort}
arms <- tibble::tribble(
  ~arm,              ~dose, ~CYP2D6_PM, ~ndays,
  "20 mg BID EM",       20,          0,      7,
  "20 mg BID PM",       20,          1,      7,
  "40 mg BID EM",       40,          0,      7,
  "40 mg BID PM",       40,          1,      7,
  "60 mg BID PM",       60,          1,     12
)
n_per_arm <- 200

make_arm <- function(i) {
  a <- arms[i, ]
  ids <- (i - 1) * n_per_arm + seq_len(n_per_arm)
  dose_times <- seq(0, by = 12, length.out = 2 * a$ndays)
  last <- max(dose_times)
  obs_times <- sort(unique(c(0, seq(0, last - 12, by = 12),
                             last + seq(0, 12, by = 0.25))))
  doses <- expand.grid(id = ids, time = dose_times)
  doses$amt <- a$dose
  doses$evid <- 1L
  obs <- expand.grid(id = ids, time = obs_times)
  obs$amt <- 0
  obs$evid <- 0L
  dplyr::bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      cmt = ifelse(evid == 1L, "depot", "central"),
      arm = a$arm,
      CYP2D6_PM = a$CYP2D6_PM,
      WT = 73,
      tlast = last
    )
}
events <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(arms)), make_arm)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))
```

Body weight is held at the 73 kg median because the paper does not print the
weight distribution of the atomoxetine trials; between-subject variability is
the Table 2 CV on CL/F only, as in the paper's inputs.

# Simulation

```{r simulate}
mod <- readModelDb("Oggianu_2020_atomoxetine")
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20200212)
sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = events,
                       keep = c("arm", "tlast")) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

# Replicate published figures

Supplementary Figures S3A and S3B show the predicted mean atomoxetine profile
after 20 mg twice daily in EM and PM subjects. The plot below shows the
simulated mean over the last dosing interval for every arm.

```{r profiles, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
sim |>
  dplyr::filter(time >= tlast) |>
  dplyr::mutate(tad = time - tlast) |>
  dplyr::group_by(arm, tad) |>
  dplyr::summarise(Cc = mean(Cc), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(tad, Cc, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Time after the last morning dose (h)",
       y = "Mean atomoxetine (ng/mL)", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Mean steady-state profiles (cf. Oggianu 2020 Figures S3A and S3B).")
```

# PKNCA validation

```{r pknca}
conc <- sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, arm, tlast)
conc <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  conc,
  conc |> dplyr::distinct(id, arm, tlast) |> dplyr::mutate(time = 0, Cc = 0)
) |>
  dplyr::distinct(id, arm, time, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, time)

dose <- events |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1L) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, amt, arm)

intervals <- conc |>
  dplyr::distinct(arm, tlast) |>
  dplyr::transmute(arm, start = tlast, end = tlast + 12,
                   cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE)

nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(
  PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc, Cc ~ time | arm + id, concu = "ng/mL", timeu = "h"),
  PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose, amt ~ time | arm + id, doseu = "mg"),
  intervals = as.data.frame(intervals)
))
nca_df <- as.data.frame(nca)
```

## Comparison against the published predictions

The paper reports arithmetic means of its virtual trials, so the simulated
individual NCA values are averaged the same way before comparison.

```{r nca-compare}
sim_means <- nca_df |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "auclast")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(arm, PPTESTCD) |>
  dplyr::summarise(PPORRES = mean(PPORRES), .groups = "drop")

published <- tibble::tribble(
  ~arm,             ~cmax, ~auclast,
  "20 mg BID EM",   171.2,   1179.6,
  "20 mg BID PM",   776.2,   8210.0,
  "40 mg BID EM",   355.1,   2025.1,
  "40 mg BID PM",  1607.7,  16601.8,
  "60 mg BID PM",  2325.5,  24196.6
)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = sim_means,
  reference = published,
  by = "arm",
  units = c(cmax = "ng/mL", auclast = "ng*h/mL"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(
  cmp,
  caption = paste("Simulated means vs. Oggianu 2020 predicted means",
                  "(Table 3; Supplementary Tables S3.1, S3.2, S3.4).",
                  "AUC is over the steady-state dosing interval.")
)
```

```{r nca-gate}
pct <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9.eE+-]", "", as.character(cmp[["% diff"]])))
)
stopifnot(
  sum(is.finite(pct)) == 10,
  # A mis-transcribed clearance, volume or B:P moves every arm by tens of
  # percent; the centre of the ten comparisons catches that.
  median(abs(pct), na.rm = TRUE) < 6,
  # The 20 mg EM AUC is the loosest row (see text); 25% bounds it.
  max(abs(pct), na.rm = TRUE) < 25
)
```

Cmax agrees within about 6% in every arm, and AUC within about 8% except in
the 20 mg EM arm. The extensive-metabolizer rows also carry the most
sampling noise: with a 55.7% CV on clearance, the mean of 200 simulated
subjects moves by several percent between seeds. A seed-free check removes
that noise. At steady state the dosing-interval AUC is `dose / (CL/F)`, so
for a log-normal CL/F whose arithmetic mean is the Table 2 value, the
population mean AUC is `dose / mean(CL/F) x (1 + CV^2)`:

```{r analytic-auc}
analytic <- published |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    clpo = ifelse(grepl("EM", arm), 26.4, 2.55),
    cv = ifelse(grepl("EM", arm), 0.557, 0.18),
    dose = as.numeric(sub(" mg.*", "", arm)),
    expected_auc = dose * 1000 / clpo * (1 + cv^2),
    pct_diff = 100 * (expected_auc / auclast - 1)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(arm, published_auc = auclast, expected_auc, pct_diff)
knitr::kable(
  analytic |>
    dplyr::rename("Arm" = arm, "Published mean AUC" = published_auc,
                  "Expected mean AUC" = expected_auc, "% diff" = pct_diff),
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Expected population-mean steady-state AUC (ng.h/mL) from the Table 2 CL/F and CV."
)
stopifnot(sum(abs(analytic$pct_diff) < 3) == 4)
```

Four arms agree within 3%. In the 20 mg EM arm the expected mean is 993
ng.h/mL against a published 1,180. The paper's trial-by-trial values for that
arm (Supplementary Table S3.1) explain the gap: nine trials range from 755 to
1,398 ng.h/mL and one (trial 7) reached 1,930 ng.h/mL, so the published mean
of 70 subjects is pulled up by the long right tail of the clearance
distribution. No parameter was tuned.

# Trazodone: why the victim model is not packaged {#trazodone}

The trazodone clearance layer *is* reproducible. Equations 1-2 back-calculate
the intrinsic clearance from the observed intravenous clearance of 10 L/h, and
the printed inputs return it:

```{r trazodone-clearance}
fup <- 0.0354
bp_t <- 0.68
clint_3a4 <- 0.438 * 137 * 39.8 * 1648 * 60 / 1e6 # uL/min/pmol -> L/h
clint_hlm <- 25.7 * 39.8 * 1648 * 60 / 1e6        # uL/min/mg   -> L/h
clint <- clint_3a4 + clint_hlm
fub <- fup / bp_t
cl_h_plasma <- bp_t * qh * fub * clint / (qh + fub * clint)
c(CLint_L_h = clint, fm_CYP3A4 = clint_3a4 / clint,
  CL_plasma_L_h = cl_h_plasma, fH = qh / (qh + fub * clint))
```

The 70% CYP3A4 share and the 10 L/h clearance both come back. The
distribution does not. Trazodone was modelled as full PBPK, so the only
distribution value in the paper is Vss = 1.0 L/kg. A one-compartment
reduction with that volume, the Table 1 ka of 1.60 1/h, and even the most
favourable availability (`F = fa x fH`, with gut availability 1) cannot
reach the paper's predicted peak:

```{r trazodone-falsifier}
ka_t <- 1.60
v_t <- 1.0 * 73
f_t <- 0.98 * qh / (qh + fub * clint)
k_t <- cl_h_plasma / v_t
tmax_t <- log(ka_t / k_t) / (ka_t - k_t)
cmax_t <- f_t * 30 / v_t * ka_t / (ka_t - k_t) *
  (exp(-k_t * tmax_t) - exp(-ka_t * tmax_t)) * 1000
c(Cmax_ng_mL = cmax_t, predicted_Cmax = 387.9,
  ratio = cmax_t / 387.9, Tmax_h = tmax_t)
```

The reduction gives about 69% of the paper's predicted 30 mg oral-solution
Cmax (387.9 ng/mL, Table 3) and a Tmax near 1.7 h, against the ~0.5 h the
paper reports for its simulations. The early peak comes from Simcyp's
multi-organ distribution, which the paper does not print, so the trazodone
model and the paediatric dose predictions built on it (Table 4) are not
reproduced here. For the same reason the atomoxetine CYP3A4 inhibition
constant (Ki = 34 uM, fu,mic = 0.23) has no victim to act on and is not
encoded.

As a rough check on the size of the effect, a basic static calculation with
the 60 mg twice-daily PM peak (unbound fraction 0.02, molecular weight 291.82)
and a 70% CYP3A4 fraction for trazodone gives a hepatic AUC ratio near 1.01:

```{r static-ddi}
i_u <- 2325.5 / 291.82 * 0.02          # unbound peak, uM
ki_u <- 34 * 0.23                      # unbound Ki, uM
1 / (0.7 / (1 + i_u / ki_u) + 0.3)
```

This ignores gut-wall inhibition, which the Simcyp prediction includes, so it
sits below the paper's predicted ratio of 1.06; both agree that no clinically
relevant interaction is expected.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Model class.** The packaged model is a compartmental reduction of a Simcyp
  minimal-PBPK model, not the platform model. Because the paper reports no
  single adjusting compartment for atomoxetine, the reduction is
  mono-exponential like the source.
* **Hepatic blood flow and liver volume.** The paper prints QH = 90 L/h and a
  liver weight of 1,648 g in the trazodone Methods; both are applied to
  atomoxetine because both compounds were simulated in the same Simcyp
  healthy-volunteer population. The liver weight is taken as 1.648 L. The
  portal-vein volume is not printed and is not subtracted.
* **Gut availability.** Table 2 gives fraction absorbed 1 and fu,gut 1 and
  enters atomoxetine clearance as an in vivo CL/F rather than as
  enzyme-specific intrinsic clearances, so gut-wall metabolism is taken as
  absent (fG = 1).
* **Renal clearance.** Not in Table 2; taken as zero, so CL/F is entirely
  hepatic.
* **Body weight.** Held at the 73 kg adult median (Table 4) in the
  validation. Simcyp samples body weight across its population; that
  distribution is not printed. Clearance is not scaled by weight, since the
  paper enters CL/F in L/h.
* **Between-subject variability.** Only the Table 2 CV on CL/F is carried,
  as a log-normal distribution whose arithmetic mean is the tabulated CL/F.
  The other sources of variability in a Simcyp population (organ sizes,
  blood flows, protein binding) are not printed and are not carried.
* **Residual error.** None (the source is a simulation model); `propSd` is
  fixed at zero.
* **CYP2D6 phenotypes.** Only extensive and poor metabolizers are
  represented, matching the paper.
* **Trazodone.** The full-PBPK trazodone model, the paediatric dose
  predictions and the trazodone interaction ratios are not reproduced (see
  above).
